title: What Can a Private Draw Tell Us About a Crowd? — Stanley Warner’s (1965) Randomized-Response Spinner, Boruch Forced-Response Likelihoods & Höglinger–Jann Individual-Level Validation Against Observed Dice-Game Cheating

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: How do you measure cheating, tax evasion, or illicit drug use when respondents lie to protect themselves? Warner's (1965) randomized response lets a private coin or spinner shield every individual's answer while simple algebra recovers the crowd's true rate.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Privacy-preserving randomization inspired modern differential privacy—yet real-world validation experiments reveal a surprising human twist when innocent people hate tossing a 'say yes' coin!
keyTakeaways: In forced-response randomized response, a private random device forces 'Yes' with known probability p1, 'No' with p0, and asks for the truthful sensitive answer with probability (1 - p1 - p0).

No interviewer can prove any single 'Yes' came from guilt rather than the coin, yet observed 'Yes' rate P(Yes) = p1 + (1 - p1 - p0)*pi solves cleanly for population prevalence pi (at the cost of higher variance).

Hoglinger and Jann's clever dice-game validation compared randomized-response estimates against *known* ground-truth cheating—exposing protective noncompliance when honest participants refuse to obey a forced 'Yes.'

vocab.meaning: Survey technique injecting known private randomness into individual answers to guarantee plausible deniability while preserving group estimability.
Mathematical protection ensuring an external observer's posterior belief about any single respondent stays bounded away from certainty.
Behavioral bias where innocent respondents disobey a random device's instruction to answer 'Yes' out of fear of looking guilty.

quiz.question: Suppose a private coin forces 'Yes' with probability 0.25 and otherwise asks truthfully (probability 0.75). If 40% of a large crowd answers 'Yes' (and everyone follows instructions), what is the estimated true prevalence pi?
